title: Math and Measurement Language
objectives: I can explain what ten math and measurement words mean.
I can use words like exact, approximate, maximum, and minimum to say how precise an answer is.
I can use the parts peri- and meter to understand the word perimeter.
I can explain my thinking in a math problem using these words.
rationale: Math word problems are written in precise language, and a student who confuses perimeter with area or exact with approximate gives wrong answers for the wrong reason. This unit gives students three named math terms (angle, symmetry, perimeter) and seven Tier 2 words that explain thinking (calculate, rotate, approximate, quantity, exact, maximum, minimum). The words are taught in pairs where they contrast (exact and approximate, maximum and minimum) and in a set that describes a shape. The passage is a class planning a garden, so students see each word used to solve a real problem.

words.def: The shape made where two lines meet.

senses.def: The direction you look at something from.
senses.example: The photo was taken from a low angle.

words.ex: A right angle looks like the corner of a book.
words.ex2: The ramp makes a small angle with the ground.
words.nonExample: A single straight line by itself is not an angle.

apps.academic: In geometry, you measure an angle in degrees.
apps.spoken: What angle does the ladder make?
apps.writing: Use angle for where two lines or sides meet, or for the direction of a view.

cloze.s: The ramp makes a small ___ with the floor, so it is easy to roll a cart up.

cloze2.s: A square corner is a right ___ and measures ninety degrees.

misuse.s: The angle of the corner told how many meters long the fence was.
misuse.why: An angle is the shape where two lines meet, measured in degrees, not a length in meters.

visual.alt: A triangle ruler beside a ladder leaning on a wall.

words.def: When two sides of a shape match like mirror images.
words.ex: A butterfly's wings show symmetry because the left side matches the right.
words.ex2: The letter A has symmetry: fold it down the middle and both sides match.
words.nonExample: A scribble that is different on each side has no symmetry.

apps.academic: In math, a line of symmetry divides a shape into two matching halves.
apps.writing: Use symmetry for matching halves, as in a face or a leaf.

cloze.s: Fold the paper heart down the middle: both halves match, so it has ___.

cloze2.s: A starfish shows ___ because its arms are arranged the same way around its center.

misuse.s: The scribble had perfect symmetry because the left and right sides looked completely different.
misuse.why: Symmetry means both sides match; sides that look different are not symmetrical.

words.def: The distance all the way around a shape.
words.ex: To find the perimeter of the garden, add the lengths of all four sides.
words.ex2: A fence around the whole yard covers its perimeter.
words.nonExample: The space inside a shape is not its perimeter.

apps.academic: In math, perimeter is measured in units such as feet or meters.
apps.spoken: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
apps.writing: Use perimeter for the distance around, and area for the space inside.

cloze.s: To fence the yard, Dad walked along the ___ and measured all four sides.

cloze2.s: The runners jogged around the ___ of the field, a distance of one hundred meters.

misuse.s: The perimeter of the rectangle is the space inside, which we cover with grass.
misuse.why: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, not the space inside it.

visual.alt: A ruler beside a green square.

words.def: To find an answer by using math.
words.ex: We calculate the cost by multiplying the price by the number of items.
words.ex2: Use a number line to calculate how many days are left before the trip.
words.nonExample: Guessing without any math is not calculating.

apps.academic: In math class, you calculate the answer and show your steps.
apps.writing: Use calculate when you use numbers and math steps to find an answer.

cloze.s: I will ___ the total cost by adding the price of each item on my list.

cloze2.s: Please ___ how much change we will get back from a ten-dollar bill.

misuse.s: He calculated the answer by guessing a number without doing any math.
misuse.why: To calculate is to use math to find an answer, not to guess.

visual.alt: An abacus beside a row of numbers.

words.def: To turn around a center point.
words.ex: Earth rotates once about every twenty-four hours.
words.ex2: Rotate the puzzle piece a quarter turn to make it fit.
words.nonExample: Sliding a shape straight across the table is not rotating it.

apps.academic: In geometry, you rotate a shape around a point and the shape stays the same size.
apps.spoken: Rotate the page to the left.
apps.writing: Use rotate for turning around a center, not for sliding or flipping.

cloze.s: The ceiling fan blades ___ so fast that they look like a blur.

cloze2.s: Turn the knob to ___ the dial until the arrow points to the red mark.

misuse.s: To rotate the paper, slide it straight across the table without turning it at all.
misuse.why: Rotate means turn around a point; sliding does not turn it.

visual.alt: A circle of arrows beside a gear.

words.def: Close to the exact amount, but not perfect.
words.ex: The approximate length of the table is two meters.
words.ex2: Give an approximate time, such as about three o'clock.
words.nonExample: A measurement taken to the exact millimeter is not approximate.

apps.academic: In math, an approximate answer is useful when an exact answer is not needed.
apps.spoken: The approximate cost is ten dollars.
apps.writing: Use approximate for close but not exact amounts.

cloze.s: A weather report gives an ___ time for the rain, such as around noon.

cloze2.s: The ___ weight of the pumpkin is ten pounds, but we did not weigh it exactly.

misuse.s: The approximate answer was perfectly exact, down to the last decimal.
misuse.why: Approximate means close but not exact.

visual.alt: A target beside a magnifying glass.

words.def: An amount of something that can be counted or measured.
words.ex: A large quantity of flour was needed for the bread.
words.ex2: Scientists measure the quantity of rain that falls each month.
words.nonExample: A color is not a quantity.

apps.academic: In science, you measure the quantity of liquid with a beaker.
apps.writing: Use quantity for how much or how many of something there is.

cloze.s: The recipe called for a large ___ of apples, enough to fill three baskets.

cloze2.s: A small ___ of salt is enough to flavor the soup.

misuse.s: A quantity is a color, such as bright red.
misuse.why: A quantity is an amount that can be counted or measured, not a color.

words.def: Completely correct, with nothing left out.
words.ex: The exact answer to eight times seven is fifty-six.
words.ex2: Please measure the exact length of the board before you cut it.
words.nonExample: A rough guess is not exact.

apps.academic: In science, you record exact measurements so others can repeat your work.
apps.writing: Use exact for completely correct, not close or rough.

cloze.s: The ___ answer to six times nine is fifty-four, not about fifty.

cloze2.s: To build the shelf, the carpenter needed the ___ length of the wall, down to the centimeter.

misuse.s: Her answer was exact because she rounded it roughly to the nearest ten.
misuse.why: Exact means completely correct; rounding roughly is not exact.

visual.alt: A dart in the center of a target beside a check mark.

words.def: The greatest amount or number possible.
words.ex: The elevator holds a maximum of ten people.
words.ex2: Today's temperature reached a maximum of ninety degrees at noon.
words.nonExample: The smallest number in a group is not the maximum.

apps.academic: In math, the maximum of a set is the largest number in it.
apps.writing: Use maximum for the greatest amount that is allowed or possible.

cloze.s: The sign says the ___ weight for the bridge is ten tons.

cloze2.s: A roller coaster reaches its ___ speed on the steepest drop.

misuse.s: The maximum number of students is the smallest number allowed in the room.
misuse.why: Maximum is the greatest amount, not the smallest.

visual.alt: An upward arrow beside a TOP sign.

words.def: The smallest amount or number possible.
words.ex: You need a minimum of two players to start the game.
words.ex2: The minimum height for the ride is forty inches.
words.nonExample: The largest number in a group is not the minimum.

apps.academic: In math, the minimum of a set is the smallest number in it.
apps.writing: Use minimum for the smallest amount that is allowed or possible.

cloze.s: To ride the roller coaster, you must be at least forty-eight inches, the ___ height.

cloze2.s: The ___ temperature last night was thirty degrees, the lowest of the whole week.

misuse.s: The minimum score was the highest score anyone could reach.
misuse.why: Minimum is the smallest amount, not the highest.

visual.alt: A downward arrow beside a down triangle.

passage.title: The Garden Plan
paras: Mrs. Park's class wanted to build a garden behind the school. First, they drew a plan. The garden would be a rectangle, and the students had to calculate how much fencing to buy. "We must know the perimeter," said Dev, "the distance all the way around."

The students measured two sides. One side was ten meters, and the other was six meters. Dev added them: ten plus six plus ten plus six equals thirty-two. "The exact perimeter is thirty-two meters," he said. Lena shrugged. "My approximate guess was thirty," she said. "Close, but not exact."

Next, they thought about the quantity of seeds they needed. The packet said the maximum number of seeds for one row is twenty and the minimum is twelve. The class decided to plant sixteen seeds in each row.

Maya drew a square corner, a right angle, where the fence would meet the school wall. "Let's make the garden show symmetry," she said. "The left side will match the right side, like a mirror." She rotated her drawing a quarter turn to see the plan from another side.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, what does the word "approximate" mean?
choices: Close to the right amount, but not exact
qs.why: Lena's guess of thirty was close to thirty-two but not exact.

choices: The distance all the way around the garden
qs.why: Dev explains it as the distance all the way around.

qs.q: Why did the class want to know the perimeter?
choices: To decide how much fencing to buy
To choose a name for the garden
qs.why: They needed to calculate how much fencing to buy, which depends on the distance around.

qs.q: Which detail shows how Dev found the exact perimeter?
choices: The packet limits seeds per row.
He added ten, six, ten, and six to get thirty-two meters.
qs.why: Adding all four sides gives the exact total.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A class used math steps and words to plan a garden.
qs.why: The class calculates, measures, and plans the garden using math ideas.

write.prompt: Describe a space you would like to plan, such as a garden or a room. Use at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: To plan my ___, I will calculate ___. The exact ___ is ___.

study.task: Break perimeter into peri- and meter, and say what each part means. Then use the two parts to explain why the word names a distance around a shape.

analogies.relation: a measure and where it is measured

sentences: Write a sentence that tells how to find the perimeter of a rectangle.
Write a sentence that uses both exact and approximate.
Write a sentence about a minimum or a maximum you have seen on a sign or a rule.
Write a sentence about an object that has symmetry.

given: The other side is six meters.
combine.model: The garden is a rectangle with one side of ten meters and the other side of six meters.
Lena's guess of thirty meters was approximate, but Dev's calculation of thirty-two meters was exact.

discuss: When is an approximate answer good enough, and when do you need an exact answer?
How are a maximum and a minimum useful in rules, like for a ride or a game?
What objects in the classroom have symmetry?
produce.explain: Explain the difference between perimeter and area. Use perimeter and give an example.

argue.prompt: Claim: Students should always calculate exact answers instead of approximate ones. Take a side and give two reasons.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. For example, ___.

constructed.prompt: A garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. Use perimeter, calculate, and exact to explain how to find how much fence you need.
constructed.model: To find the perimeter, I calculate by adding all four sides: 8 plus 5 plus 8 plus 5. The exact perimeter is 26 meters, so I need 26 meters of fence.

constructed.prompt: A sign says a bus holds a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 40 riders. Explain what each word tells you and what quantity of riders is not allowed.
look: uses both maximum and minimum correctly
states that fewer than 5 or more than 40 riders is not allowed by the sign
constructed.model: The minimum is the smallest number of riders, 5. The maximum is the greatest number, 40. A quantity of 41 riders or 3 riders would not follow the sign.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten math words, pair them where they contrast (exact and approximate, maximum and minimum), and use them to plan a garden. They break the word perimeter into its Greek parts and see how the parts explain the meaning.

notes.va.angle.n: Show a book corner and a ramp. Students often think an angle is only a shape, not the opening between lines. Link to degrees for measuring. The sense of a view is a second use.
notes.va.symmetry.n: Fold paper to test: if the halves match, it has symmetry. Students may call any pattern symmetrical; ask them to show the fold line.
notes.va.perimeter.n: Peri- (around) + meter (measure). Contrast with area on a grid: walk the edge for perimeter, shade the inside for area.
notes.va.calculate.v: Calculate means to use math to find an answer. Contrast with guess. Ask students to show steps in a short explanation.
notes.va.rotate.v: Use a cutout shape on a pin. Contrast with slide and flip. Link to Earth's rotation in science.
notes.va.approximate.adj: Ask when a close answer is enough, such as how long until lunch. The word is also a verb in some uses; this unit teaches the adjective.
notes.va.quantity.n: Quantity is how much or how many. Use a beaker and counters. Ask students what quantity of water fills a cup.
notes.va.exact.adj: Exact means completely correct. Use a ruler to measure a pencil and show the difference between about 15 cm and exactly 15.2 cm.
notes.va.maximum.n: The greatest amount allowed or possible. Use a sign, such as a bridge limit. Students sometimes reverse maximum and minimum; use max for most and min for least as a memory cue.
notes.va.minimum.n: The smallest amount allowed or possible. Pair with maximum on a number line. Practice with rules like a minimum height for a ride.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The garden is ten by six. Perimeter is the distance all the way around, so I add ten, six, ten, and six. That is thirty-two, an exact answer. If I only said about thirty, that would be approximate. I can tell from the words which one the problem wants.'
discuss: Which word in this unit is most useful in a math problem?
How do the parts peri- and meter help you remember perimeter?
misconceptions: Perimeter and area mean the same thing.
A minimum is the biggest number.
A rotation is the same as a slide.
extend: Plan a classroom garden with a perimeter, a quantity of seeds, and a maximum and minimum for each row.
Find symmetry in letters, shapes, and nature and make a poster.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the exact and approximate pair and the maximum and minimum pair two days later with quick word problems. At one week, mix perimeter, calculate, and quantity in a real task.

My answer is exact because ___. Your answer is approximate because ___.

wida.oral: Partner A states a math situation, such as a fence or a ride sign. Partner B names the math word that fits and explains why.
